content.title: The Earliest Muslim Women
paragraphs: Chapter Seven
The Earliest Muslim Women

The previous chapter ended with a small community forming around the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: men and women, free people and enslaved people, adults and young people. If we look more closely at this community, we find that the story of Islam at its beginning was never a story of men alone. Women were present from the very first moment revelation began.

Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, was the first person to believe the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and affirm his message. The first human name to enter the story of Islam after the Messenger of Allah is therefore the name of a woman. As the circle widened, other women also chose faith at a time when Muslims were neither a powerful group that promised safety nor a large community that a new believer could easily shelter behind.
Years later, when the Qur’an spoke of what believers had given through migration, suffering, and sacrifice, its wording included men and women together:

Their Lord responded to them: “I will never waste the deeds of any doer among you, male or female; you are the same in reward. Those who migrated and were driven out of their homes and suffered for My sake, and fought and were killed – I will surely expiate their sins and admit them into gardens under which rivers flow, a reward from Allah; with Allah is the best reward.”
Qur’an 3:195 — Rowwad Translation Center (QuranEnc)

This verse was revealed in Madinah, after the Makkan stage we are now following, but its words describe with precision what many women of the first generation would do: they would believe, suffer harm, leave their homes and lands for their faith, and Allah would not let their deeds be lost.

Umm Ayman, may Allah be pleased with her, had known the Prophet from his childhood and later became one of the early Muslims. Her name was Barakah. She was of Abyssinian origin and was known as one of those who cared for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when he was a child. Biographical works report that she had been attached to the household of ‘Abdullah, the Prophet’s father, and later became part of the Prophet’s household and was freed. In this setting, a freedwoman was someone who had once lived under slavery and was then set free, while a social bond of loyalty remained between her and the household that freed her.

Umm Ayman, may Allah be pleased with her, lived through an extraordinary transition. She knew Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as a child, then saw him become a man and then a prophet. She believed in him and became one of the early believers. She would later migrate with the Muslims, and she and her family would continue to appear in the events of the Seerah. She was the mother of Ayman ibn ‘Ubayd, and later married Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, and gave birth to Usamah ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him. A woman who had been close to the Prophetic household since his childhood chose faith when that choice had become costly.

In another Makkan household lived Lubabah al-Kubra, may Allah be pleased with her, better known by her kunyah, Umm al-Fadl. A kunyah is an Arabic form of address such as “mother of so-and-so.” She was the wife of al-‘Abbas ibn ‘Abd al-Muttalib, the Prophet’s uncle. Ibn Sa‘d reports that she was among the earliest women to accept Islam after Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, while the Seerah sources differ over exactly who came first after Khadijah.

Another woman who accepted Islam early was Fatimah bint al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with her, the sister of ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab. She and her husband Sa‘id ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him, accepted Islam before ‘Umar did. Later, her own home would become an important place in the story of her brother’s conversion. Sometimes faith entered a household through a woman before it entered through a man who would later become one of Islam’s most famous figures.

Not every woman who accepted Islam had the protection of a strong family or tribe. Some enslaved women in Makkah — women living under slavery and lacking full control over their own lives — entered Islam and were tortured because of their faith. Their owners could harm them without a powerful tribe standing behind them to intervene.

The Seerah sources preserve the names of some of these women instead of leaving them anonymous: Zinnirah, al-Nahdiyyah and her daughter, Umm ‘Ubays, and a slave woman from Banu Mu’ammal. Reports of the Seerah state that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, purchased a number of vulnerable and persecuted believers who were being tortured because of Islam and then freed them; these women were among them. Manumission means freeing a person from slavery so that he or she becomes free.

One of the best-known of these accounts is that of Zinnirah, may Allah be pleased with her. She was among the early Muslims and was tortured, and her eyesight was affected. Some polytheists claimed that al-Lat and al-‘Uzza — two of the Arabs’ idols — had caused her blindness. She rejected that belief and remained firm in faith. Seerah reports state that her sight later returned, and the polytheists then explained that by calling it “Muhammad’s magic.” The incident shows something of the atmosphere believers lived in: when hardship struck, opponents attributed it to the idols; when the hardship disappeared, they searched for another explanation that allowed them to continue rejecting the message.

Sumayyah bint Khayyat, may Allah be pleased with her, gives the clearest picture of how high the price of faith could become. As described in the previous chapter, she was among the vulnerable believers and would become the first martyr in Islam, according to the well-known and established reports of the Seerah scholars. She accepted Islam in a time of weakness, without a powerful tribe to shield her from harm, and remained firm until she was killed.

So at the very beginning we see two images that cannot be overlooked: the first person to believe the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, and the first martyr in Islam was a woman, Sumayyah, may Allah be pleased with her. Between these two women stand many other names, each carrying faith according to her own circumstances.

Some of the early believing women also came from the homes of Quraysh’s leading families. Faith did not automatically follow the position of a father, husband, or tribe. A striking example is Umm Kulthum bint ‘Uqbah ibn Abi Mu‘ayt, may Allah be pleased with her. Her father was among those who harmed the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, most severely, yet his daughter accepted Islam. Years later, after the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, she would migrate to Madinah on her own, and her relatives would try to have her returned. Her household’s opposition did not prevent her from choosing her faith.

A woman’s choice of faith despite her family’s opposition is especially clear in the story of Ramlah bint Abi Sufyan, may Allah be pleased with her, better known as Umm Habibah. Her father Abu Sufyan was at that time one of the leaders of Quraysh, but she accepted Islam and later migrated to Abyssinia with her husband ‘Ubaydullah ibn Jahsh. Seerah works report that her husband became a Christian there and left Islam while she remained firm in her faith, although the reliability of the account of his conversion is disputed. Later Allah would honor her by making her a wife of the Messenger of Allah. Her life shows that a woman’s faith in the first generation was not simply a reflection of the choice made by the man beside her.

Then the migration to Abyssinia revealed a new kind of sacrifice. Migration means leaving one country for another in order to protect one’s faith. The journey from Makkah to Abyssinia was not a short or comfortable trip. It meant leaving family and homeland, moving to another land among another people, and crossing the sea using the means of travel available at the time.

Among the earliest women to undergo this experience was Ruqayyah, may Allah be pleased with her, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, together with her husband ‘Uthman ibn ‘Affan, may Allah be pleased with him. Even the Prophet’s own household was not spared the cost of the call. His daughter would leave the Makkah where she had been born to live as a stranger in a distant land for the sake of her faith.

Layla bint Abi Hathmah, may Allah be pleased with her, was also among the women who migrated to Abyssinia, together with her husband ‘Amir ibn Rabi‘ah, may Allah be pleased with him. Many other women may be unfamiliar to the reader, yet the biographical and Seerah works repeatedly describe them with brief phrases such as “she accepted Islam early” and “she migrated to the land of Abyssinia.” Those short phrases hide difficult decisions: going against society, leaving home, enduring travel, and living in a foreign land.

Being among the first women to accept Islam required courage and sacrifice. An early believing woman in those days was entering a faith whose followers were still few. Her belief might provoke her family, owner, or tribe. And when migration followed, she had to leave the place she knew for a land she had never lived in before.

These women did not all share the same social position. Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, was a woman of wealth and status. Zinnirah and Umm ‘Ubays were among the vulnerable. Ruqayyah, may Allah be pleased with her, was the Prophet’s daughter. Umm Habibah, may Allah be pleased with her, was the daughter of one of Quraysh’s leaders. Umm Ayman was an Abyssinian woman who had lived in the Prophetic household from long before. Their different homes and origins did not prevent them from sharing the same faith.

As more men and women entered Islam, Makkah began to see that this call had gone beyond one household or a narrow circle of friends. It had followers from different clans of Quraysh, from different social classes, and among both men and women. The confrontation mentioned at the end of the previous chapter was drawing closer.

For the leaders of Quraysh, the problem was no longer simply that Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was saying something new. The problem was that people were believing him, their number was growing, and some of them did not turn back even when they paid a real price. From this point, the Seerah moves into a new stage: how would Quraysh try to stop the call before it spread further?
Sources

Sources: Qur’an 3:195. Biographical accounts: Ibn Sa‘d and Ibn Hisham. On Barakah, known as Umm Ayman, her background, care for the Prophet, and migration: al-Mizzi, Tahdhib al-Kamal. Reports of the persecuted women freed by Abu Bakr, including Zinnirah, al-Nahdiyyah, and Umm ‘Ubays: reports of Ibn Ishaq and material transmitted by Ibn al-Athir in al-Kamil. Ruqayyah’s migration with ‘Uthman to Abyssinia: Seerah and biographical works, including al-Dhahabi’s Siyar A‘lam al-Nubala’. The account of Umm Habibah’s husband becoming Christian and of her steadfastness appears in biographical works and al-Mustadrak, including reports through al-Zuhri; the report of his conversion is disputed. For an assessment of its chains of transmission: IslamQA, answer 459340. Reports differ over the exact order of women who accepted Islam after Khadijah, so no absolute sequence is imposed.
